chapter: Theater work, first jobs and recording credits
title: Teaching today and the Regal pit under Erskine Tate
summary: He describes his students and theater playing, watching Erskine Tate's baton.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Yeah. I'm teaching Chicago, I have pupils. And that's my theory. I'd rather have them make one nice round good tone than six bad ones. Now I have one fella, he's got a nice big tone already. He's been trying to teach himself. His name is David Mertz. And so he's been under my wing about two months now. And the only trouble he has is say like one, two, three, four. He has trouble just keeping time with his feet. Well I can play and I just don't have to pat my feet. Yeah, he was falling in the middle of the thing. You understand? I just count up here. You understand? So he's coming along pretty good. So when these fellas realized anything, I had caught up with them and passed them. Cat Garland and a lot of guys, ace trombone players around, they had a fella called Happy, he played with his foot. Yeah, and the brunners can do that too, you know. And so the brunners lay on his back and play his own. And so I gave everybody credit. I didn't try to take anything away. I just try to get as good as I can, you understand? And so when I fell into the regal alley, some of them actually attended the first show. Man, it was, music is music universally. You understand what I'm talking about? I mean there's no reason why, if a fella's a good musician, one type of musician would work, not if you get a rehearsal, get the exact time or a nice rehearsal, you see what I'm talking about. March, overtures, anything like that. The brass band has brought me out to marches and things because I found out when I went in the theater, I had to play those things, see. And they have different things like, one they want you double faulty, double fist, and they cut out, sometimes they cut you out very quick. Now you've got to watch the stick. See, you may get twelve eighths times, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, twelve, and then he come down again, one, two. You may get six eighths, you may play six eighths like this, one, two like that, and you get one of the things, I forget what you call that, it's real fast, you know, on two, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, like that. Then you may get your one, two, one, two, one, two, three, one, two, three, and like that. And then you may get, he may give you four. Well you have to notice that stick, because Erskine Tate was good on that. He'd give you a silly grin when you get the, yeah, you know what I'm saying? He'd look at, he wouldn't swear at you anything, he'd just look at you and grin. And when he did like this, he'd cut you out, and you turn your music with a segue right now, right into something else, that's the way those pictures were. You know what I'm talking about? But you had to watch him. He said if he was wrong, and you with him, well you okay.

But you watch the stick. And I see a lot of fellas that used to get out there in the deep, we call it out in the deep water, and they call WP Pound Plenty, and things like that. But when he do this, that means give y'all triple 40, and then you see him, one of those things, for sound, you know, boom, you know. And just like a double P, you start off, you know, and you get to, when you get to the, to your top volume, well you just come right on back to where you started, you know. It's a term for that. And so he had, one time he had me this low effort. He, I didn't get a chance to, between shows, between pitches, I didn't get a chance to beat my chick, because he didn't like the way I was playing and making that note. So we had Bob Schottman to stand over me, the whole time in between the pitches. Bob, Bob, Bob, Bob, Bob, Bob, just that one move. Be satisfied with everything but that one move. Yeah, I had some tough time. I mean, I had some tough time.
